What is the difference between a class, an object and a reference?

A class is the definition, loaded once by a class loader. An object is an instance on the heap with its own field values. A reference is a value held in a variable that locates an object. Variables never hold objects, so assigning one to another copies the reference, and == compares references. Two objects can be equal in content but different in identity.
What happens in memory on Emp e = new Emp("Ann");?

If needed, Emp and its parents are loaded and initialized. Space is allocated, usually by a pointer bump in the thread's TLAB in Eden. The memory is zeroed, the header is written, and the constructor chain runs: Object up top first, then each class's field initializers, instance blocks and constructor body. The reference is stored in local variable e, which sits in the current stack frame. The literal "Ann" is a pooled String object referenced from the field.
How much memory does new Object() take? What about a class with one int, and one with an int and a long?

On typical 64-bit HotSpot with compressed class pointers: new Object() is 16 bytes (12-byte header plus 4 padding). A class with one int is also 16, since the int fills the padding. int plus long is 24: header 12, int 4, long 8. These are implementation details, not guarantees. JOL gives exact numbers, and Java 25's optional compact headers change them. This is why an Integer[] costs much more than an int[].
Does Java always call a constructor when creating an object?

No. clone() copies without calling one. Java deserialization skips constructors of Serializable classes, calling only the no-argument constructor of the first non-serializable parent. Records are the exception: they always go through the canonical constructor. Internal tools such as Objenesis also bypass constructors. This is why validation in constructors can be bypassed by old-style deserialization.
Why does this fail to compile? class T { T(int a) { } } class U extends T { }

Declaring T(int) removes T's default constructor. U gets a generated U() { super(); }, and there is no T() to call. Fix it by adding a T(), or by giving U a constructor calling super(0). This also matters to JPA and Jackson, which often need a no-argument constructor.
Can you use both this() and super() in one constructor? Can a constructor call an overridable method?

Not both: each must be the first statement up to Java 24, and in Java 25 a constructor still has at most one explicit constructor call. A this(...) chain ends in a constructor that calls super(...). Calling an overridable method compiles but is dangerous: the subclass version runs before subclass fields are initialized. The example above printed area=0.0. Make such methods private, final, or move the call to a factory.
What is the difference between protected and package-private? What is the trap with protected?

Package-private means same package only. protected adds subclasses in other packages. The trap: from another package, a subclass may access the protected member only through its own type, not through a parent-typed reference. Inside class T extends ArrayList<String> in another package, otherList.removeRange(0, 1) fails with "has protected access". Also, protected is often overused: it is part of your public API for anyone who subclasses.
What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

Abstraction is about the interface: which operations are exposed, so the caller thinks in terms of "send payment" rather than HTTP retries. Encapsulation is about protection: internal state can only change through controlled paths, so invariants hold. You can have one without the other: a class with public setters for everything may offer an abstraction yet have no encapsulation. Abstraction is design, and encapsulation is enforcement, typically through access modifiers.
Why does Java not support multiple inheritance of classes? How do you share code across hierarchies?

Two parents would raise questions about duplicate fields, which constructor runs, and which method wins. Java allows a single superclass but multiple interfaces, since interfaces carry no instance state. Default methods add behaviour, with the conflict rules that a class wins, then the most specific interface, and otherwise you must override. To share code otherwise, use composition: hold a helper object and delegate to it.
Is it overriding or hiding? class A { static void f() {} } class B extends A { static void f() {} }

Hiding. Static methods bind at compile time on the declared type, so A x = new B(); x.f(); calls A.f. @Override on it fails. An instance method cannot replace a static one or the reverse; both are compile errors. Fields are also hidden rather than overridden.
Output of the hiding example? Base b = new Sub(); print(b.name); print(b.sm()); print(b.im()); print(b.getName()); print(b.callPv());

base
Base.sm
Sub.im
base
Base.pv
Field access and static calls use the static type Base. Only im() dispatches dynamically. getName() is inherited code that reads Base.name. callPv() calls the private Base.pv, because private methods are not overridden, so Sub.pv is unrelated.
Output? An an = new Dg(); print(h(an)); print(h(new Dg())); with h(An) and h(Dg).
An then Dg. Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared type of the argument, regardless of the runtime object. Runtime type only matters for the receiver of a call.
Output? V1 v = new V2(); v.who(new Dg()); where V2 overrides who(An) and adds who(Dg).

V2.An. The compiler only looks at V1 and picks who(An), the sole candidate. At runtime the vtable finds V2's override of that signature. who(Dg) is never considered because it is not visible through a V1 reference. Java has single dispatch: the receiver's runtime type matters, the arguments' runtime types do not.
Can an overriding method have a different return type, throw different exceptions, or change access?

Return type: same or a subclass for references, identical for primitives and void. Exceptions: only the same or narrower checked exceptions, or none. Any unchecked ones are fine. Access: same or wider. Note that throws RuntimeException in an override is always allowed, and a method calling through a parent reference must handle the parent's declared checked exceptions even if the override declares none.
How do covariant return types work at the bytecode level?

The JVM identifies a method by name and full descriptor, including return type. So Ch self() does not override Pa self() at JVM level. javac generates a synthetic bridge method Pa self() in Ch that forwards to the new one. Reflection on Ch shows both, with isBridge() true on the generated one. Generics rely on the same trick: compareTo(Emp) gets a bridge compareTo(Object) that casts, which is where a surprise ClassCastException can come from.
Which overload runs for g(null)?

With g(Object) and g(String): String, being more specific. With Object, CharSequence and String: still String. With g(String) and g(Integer): compile error, because neither is a subtype of the other. Resolve with a cast, g((String) null).
Explain how a virtual call is dispatched, and why overriding costs almost nothing.

invokevirtual names a method, which resolves to a vtable index. At runtime the JVM takes the object's class pointer, reads that index, and jumps there. Interface calls search an itable. After warm-up the JIT uses class hierarchy analysis and type profiles to inline calls guarded by a cheap type check. A site that has seen one or two types is typically inlined; a megamorphic site keeps a table lookup. If a newly loaded class invalidates an assumption, the JVM deoptimizes back to the interpreter and recompiles.
Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can it have no abstract methods? Can it implement an interface without implementing the methods?

Yes to all three. The constructor runs through super(...) from subclasses and initializes shared state. An abstract class with no abstract methods simply cannot be instantiated: HttpServlet is an example. An abstract class implementing an interface can leave methods unimplemented for concrete subclasses to complete.
Why were default methods added? What is their danger?

Java 8 needed to add methods such as Collection.stream() to existing interfaces without breaking every implementation. A default method provides a body that implementers inherit. The danger is that a default can conflict with an implementer's assumptions, as with Collection.removeIf and synchronizedCollection-style wrappers that need their own locking, so a default can be silently wrong for an existing class. Default methods add behaviour, and they cannot add state, so they should be built from the other interface methods.
Can an interface default method override toString? Can a class call a static interface method through itself?

Neither. A default overriding an Object method is a compile error ("default method toString in interface T overrides a member of java.lang.Object"), since a class method always wins, so such a default could never run. Static interface methods are not inherited: from an implementer, write A.s(), not T.s() or this.s(). This avoids conflicts when a class implements several interfaces.
Two interfaces have the same default method. What must the class do? What if one is abstract?

In both cases the class must override, or it fails to compile. With two defaults the error is "inherits unrelated defaults". With a default and an abstract, the class is told to implement the abstract method. Inside the override, A.super.hi() selects an interface's version. If the same method is inherited from a class, the class version wins and no override is needed.
Why is Comparator a functional interface although it declares compare and equals?

Abstract methods matching public Object methods do not count, because every implementation inherits them from Object. Comparator therefore has one real abstract method. Its many other methods, such as reversed and thenComparing, are default or static.
When is composition better than inheritance? Give a concrete failure of inheritance.

Default to composition, and use inheritance only for true IS-A when the parent is designed for it. A concrete failure: a HashSet subclass counting additions, overriding add and addAll, reports 6 after adding 3 elements, since addAll internally calls add. The subclass depends on a parent implementation detail. Inheritance also exposes all parent methods, as with Stack extends Vector, which allows insertion in the middle of a stack. Composition with an interface avoids both and allows swapping the implementation in tests.
Association vs aggregation vs composition? Show the difference in code.
Static nested vs inner class? Why can an inner class leak memory?

A static nested class is a normal class scoped inside another, with no outer instance. An inner class has a hidden reference to its enclosing object. If the inner object lives longer than the outer, such as an anonymous listener or a task on a queue, the outer object cannot be collected. Lambdas capture this only if they use it, so they avoid that when they touch no instance members. Default to static.
Can an anonymous class have a constructor? Can it implement two interfaces?

Neither. It has no name, so no constructor can be declared, though arguments can go to the parent's constructor, and an instance initializer block handles setup. It can extend one class or implement one interface. A local class is the alternative when you need more. The "double brace initialization" idiom (new ArrayList<>() {{ add(1); }}) creates an anonymous subclass holding the outer reference, so avoid it.
Why must captured local variables be effectively final?

A local variable lives in a stack frame, which may be gone by the time the lambda or inner class runs. So the value is copied into the object. If the variable could then change, the copy and the original would diverge silently, and concurrent code would race. The compiler enforces it instead. Fields are different: the lambda captures this, and reads the field through it.
How are enums implemented? Why is == safe on them?

An enum compiles to a class extending Enum with one public static final instance per constant, created in a static initializer. Since instances are unique per class loader, cannot be created with new or reflection, and deserialize back to the same object by name, reference equality works. == is null-safe and checked at compile time: comparing different enum types is an error, whereas equals would just return false.
Can an enum have a constructor, abstract methods, implement an interface, or extend a class?

Constructor: yes, implicitly private. Abstract methods: yes, with each constant providing a body, which creates an anonymous subclass, so getClass() differs from getDeclaringClass(). Interfaces: yes. Extending a class: no, because it already extends Enum. Enums also cannot be extended by normal classes.
Why can an enum constructor not read a static field of the same enum?

Static initialization runs top to bottom, and constants come first, so a constructor runs before any other static fields are initialized. javac rejects it: "illegal reference to static field from initializer". Compile-time constants are allowed, since they have no runtime initialization. For a lookup map, fill it in a static block, which runs after all constants exist.
Why are EnumSet and EnumMap faster than HashSet and HashMap?

EnumSet is a bit vector, so contains, add and set operations are single bitwise instructions. EnumMap is an array indexed by ordinal(). Neither hashes or handles collisions, memory is minimal, and iteration follows declaration order. EnumSet.of returned java.util.RegularEnumSet for a small enum. A larger enum uses JumboEnumSet. Collections.synchronizedSet is needed for shared mutable use.
Records: what is a compact constructor? How is it different from a canonical one?

A canonical constructor has one parameter per component. A compact one is a shorter form of it, with no parameter list, and the compiler assigns the fields at the end. Use it for validation and normalization by reassigning the parameter: items = List.copyOf(items);. Writing this.items = ... there is an error. Any non-canonical constructor must start by calling another constructor of the record.
Are records truly immutable? Can you use one as a HashMap key, a JPA entity, or a Jackson DTO?

Shallowly immutable: a component List can still change, and that alters hashCode, so copy defensively if using a record as a key. A record with immutable components makes an excellent key. JPA entity: no, entities need a no-argument constructor, mutable fields and subclassable proxies, though records work for projections and, with Hibernate 6.2+, as embeddables. Jackson: yes, since 2.12.
Compare record equality with hand-written equals. What surprises exist?

Both are field-based, and record equality uses all components. Surprises: double and float use Double.compare semantics, so new D(NaN).equals(new D(NaN)) is true and 0.0 differs from -0.0. Arrays compare by reference. And the hashCode algorithm is deliberately unspecified, so do not persist it.
What problem do sealed classes solve? Sealed vs final vs package-private?

They let a library say "these are all the variants" while keeping the type public. final permits no subclasses. Package-private parents hide the type from users, who then cannot name it. Sealed keeps the type usable but closes extension, so the compiler can check exhaustive switches, and a new variant produces compile errors at every switch. Use them for modelling states and results: Payment, Result = Success | Failure, AST nodes.
Why might it be better not to write default in a switch over a sealed type?

Without default, the compiler checks that all permitted types are handled. Adding a new type then breaks compilation at each switch, which is what you want. A default silences that check and sends the new type to a generic path. Without it, the compiler adds a hidden throwing branch in case classes get out of sync at runtime, which produces MatchException.
What is the scope of the binding variable in o instanceof String s?

Flow-sensitive: it is in scope wherever the compiler proves the test was true. So it works after &&, inside the if, and after an if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;. It does not work after || or in the else branch of a positive test. It may shadow a field, but it cannot redeclare an existing local: with a local s, it is a compile error.
Name all methods of Object. Why are wait and notify there and not on Thread?

equals, hashCode, toString, getClass, clone, finalize, notify, notifyAll, and three overloads of wait: 11 non-private methods. Reflection on Java 21 confirms the list. wait and notify are on Object because a thread waits on a monitor, which is owned by an object, not by a thread. Any object can be a lock, so they apply to any object.
If two objects have the same hashCode, are they equal? If equals is true, must hash codes match?

Same hash does not imply equal: "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112. Equal objects must have equal hash codes; that is the contract. Returning a constant such as 1 is legal, but it puts all entries in one bucket and destroys performance. Breaking the contract makes HashMap lookups miss.
What goes wrong if you override only equals? Only hashCode?

Only equals: equal objects get different identity hashes, so a HashSet stores duplicates and map.get(equalKey) misses. Verified: two equal NoHash objects gave a set size of 2. Only hashCode: equal-looking objects land in the same bucket, but equals still uses identity, so they stay separate. List.contains uses only equals, so hash-based and list-based lookups can disagree.
public boolean equals(Employee o) compiles. What is wrong with it?

It overloads rather than overrides equals(Object). Collections call the Object version through Object-typed parameters, so they use identity, while a direct call with an Employee argument uses your method. The same two objects can look equal or unequal depending on the call site. @Override turns this into a compile error.
getClass or instanceof in equals?

instanceof allows subclass instances, which is correct for final classes or when subclasses add no state, and it works with proxies. getClass demands an exact class, keeps symmetry when subclasses add fields, but breaks the Liskov principle and fails with Hibernate proxies. A value class should normally be final, which makes the debate moot. Defining equality for a type family, as List does, means instanceof on the interface with the contract documented.
Should an entity's hashCode include a generated ID? What do you do with JPA entities?

A generated ID is null before persist and set afterward, so a hash based on it changes while the object is in a HashSet, losing the entry. Options: (1) a natural immutable key, such as an ISBN; (2) a UUID assigned at construction; (3) equals on a non-null ID and a hashCode that returns a constant per class, accepting bucket collisions in rare large sets. Use Hibernate.getClass or instanceof so that proxies compare correctly.
Shallow vs deep copy? Why is clone() considered broken?

A shallow copy duplicates the object's fields, so referenced objects are shared. A deep copy also duplicates what they reference. clone() is criticized because Cloneable has no method and merely changes Object.clone's behaviour; it skips constructors; it cannot reset final fields to copies; it throws a checked exception; and it depends on all parents cooperating. Copy constructors and factories avoid every one of these. clone() remains fine for arrays, where int[] even has a public, covariant one.
Why was finalize deprecated, and what replaces it?

It offers no guarantee of when or whether it runs, swallows exceptions, delays collection, permits resurrection, and is a security hole on partially constructed objects. The replacement is deterministic: AutoCloseable with try-with-resources. Cleaner is a backstop for a forgotten close(). It uses phantom references, so the cleaning action cannot reach the object, and must not reference it. Status: deprecated in 9 and for removal since 18.
Is this class immutable? final class H { private final List<String> l; H(List<String> l) { this.l = l; } List<String> l() { return l; } }

No. final only fixes the reference. The caller keeps the original list and can modify it, and the getter hands out the same list. Fix with this.l = List.copyOf(l);, which makes an unmodifiable copy, and the getter is then safe. Collections.unmodifiableList(l) alone is not enough, because the view reflects changes to l. If elements are mutable, they need the same treatment.
Why is String final? What if an immutable class is not final?

A non-final class allows a subclass that adds mutable state or overrides methods to lie. Code receiving a String parameter can trust it because no subclass can exist. Security checks, class loading and the pool all rely on it. Alternatives to final are a private constructor with factories, or sealing.
When does a cast fail at compile time vs at runtime?

Compile time: the types can never be related, such as two unrelated classes, or a final class and an interface it does not implement. Runtime: the cast is possible but the object is the wrong type, giving ClassCastException. A non-final class to an interface compiles, because a subclass could implement it. (Runnable) new ArrayList<String>() compiles and fails at runtime. (Runnable) Integer.valueOf(1) does not compile. The message names both classes and their loaders, which is useful when the same class name is loaded twice.
Which singleton implementation would you choose today, and how would you break the others?

An enum, if the singleton needs no parent class and early-ish creation is fine; a holder class if it must extend something. In an application, let Spring manage one bean instead. Breaking: reflection's setAccessible calls a private constructor; deserialization produces a copy unless there is readResolve; clone copies if available; a separate class loader gets its own statics. Enum defeats reflection and serialization.
Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

The first null check is outside the lock. Without volatile the write to instance can be seen before the object's constructor effects, so a reader skips the lock and gets a partly initialized object. volatile creates a happens-before edge, and forbids that reordering. It requires the Java 5+ memory model. A holder class gives the same laziness with no explicit synchronization.
Spring singleton vs GoF singleton?

GoF: one instance per class loader, enforced by the class itself through a private constructor, accessed by a static method. Spring: one instance per bean definition per ApplicationContext, enforced by the container. The class stays an ordinary class, so tests can create others or inject mocks. You can define two beans of the same class. Spring beans must be stateless or thread-safe, since all threads share them.
Scenario: a processPayment method has a long if (type == CARD) ... else if (type == UPI) .... How would you redesign it?

If new types are added often, by different teams: a PaymentProcessor strategy interface with one implementation per type, and a Map<PaymentType, PaymentProcessor> filled by Spring injection. Adding a type then means adding one class (Open/Closed). If the type set is closed, and operations are added more often: a sealed Payment hierarchy with records, and exhaustive pattern switches so the compiler finds all sites. An enum with constant-specific bodies suits very small behaviour differences. Pick based on which axis changes.
Scenario: a shared base class BaseService has grown to 2,000 lines, and every change breaks some subclass. What do you do?

That is the fragile base class problem. Steps: identify which groups of methods each subclass really uses; extract each group into a small collaborator class with an interface (auditing, validation, mapping); inject those into subclasses via constructors; move subclasses over one at a time, with characterization tests; and finally delete the base class or reduce it to a Template Method that is final except for declared extension points. Result: high cohesion, lower coupling, and collaborators that are testable alone.
A class has private fields with a public getter and setter for each. Is it encapsulated?

Only in form. If every field has a setter, any caller can still put the object into any state, and the representation is still exposed through the API. Real encapsulation means protecting invariants: expose behaviour (withdraw(amount)) rather than raw setters (setBalance), return unmodifiable views or copies of internal collections, validate in constructors, and leave out setters that are not needed. Getters and setters are still fine on DTOs and framework-bound classes, because there they are the point.
What is the "constant interface" anti-pattern?

It means declaring an interface that holds only constants (interface Config { int TIMEOUT = 30; }) and having classes implements it so they can use the names without a prefix. The constants then become part of the class's public type, so every subclass inherits them and you cannot remove them later without breaking compatibility. Put constants in a final class with a private constructor, or in an enum if they form a set, and use import static for short names. In Spring, prefer @ConfigurationProperties for values that change between environments.
Records vs Lombok @Value / @Data: which should you use?

- record: a language feature with no annotation processor. It is immutable, has component-based equals/hashCode, cannot extend a class, and has no builder. Its accessors are name(), not getName().
- @Value: similar immutability, but with getX() accessors. It can be combined with @Builder and @With, and it suits classes that need JavaBean naming.
- @Data: mutable, with setters and all-field equals/hashCode. Never use it on JPA entities.
For new DTOs and value objects on Java 17+, prefer records. Use Lombok when you need builders for many optional fields, JavaBean-style accessors for older libraries, or mutable entities (@Getter/@Setter only).
What does "program to an interface, not an implementation" mean in practice?

Declare variables, fields, parameters and return types with the most abstract type that offers the operations you need: List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(), Map rather than HashMap, and PaymentGateway rather than StripeGateway. The implementation can then change without touching callers, tests can pass fakes or mocks, and Spring can inject a proxy (for @Transactional) or another bean. Do not overdo it: an interface with only one implementation that will never change adds ceremony with no benefit, and Spring can proxy classes through CGLIB anyway.
Why might a team prefer static factories over public constructors for value types?

A factory can validate and normalize before the object exists (trimming or lower-casing an email). It can cache common instances (Money.ZERO, or Integer.valueOf for small values). It can return Optional or a subtype. Its name documents the intent (Duration.ofMinutes(5) vs new Duration(300, 0)). With a private constructor, the class controls every instance, which is how java.time and List.of keep their implementation classes hidden and free to change.
private vs static vs final methods: which can be overridden, and how is each call bound?

| private | static | final | Plain instance
Inherited | No | Yes (callable through the subclass) | Yes | Yes
Subclass same signature | A new, unrelated method | Hides the parent's (static only) | Compile error | Overrides
Which body runs | Always this class's | Chosen from the static type | Only one exists | Chosen from the runtime class
@Override allowed | No | No | Not in a subclass | Yes
Rule of thumb: only non-private, non-static, non-final instance methods are polymorphic. Put @Override on every override so the compiler catches a "hide" or a new overload you did not mean.
Telescoping constructors vs JavaBean setters vs Builder: how do you build an object with many fields?

| Telescoping constructors | No-arg + setters | Builder
Readability at call site | Poor: new Visit(id, null, true, 3) | Good | Good: named steps
Immutability | Possible | No | Yes
Valid after creation | Yes | Not until every setter is called | Yes: build() validates once
Optional fields | One constructor per combination | Easy | Easy
Cost | Little code | Little code | Extra class (or Lombok @Builder)
Visit v = Visit.builder()
    .patientId(42)
    .type(VisitType.OUTPATIENT)
    .urgent(true)
    .build();   // checks required fields here
Rule of thumb: up to three or four required fields, use a constructor or a record. Many optional fields: use a builder. Setters fit frameworks that need them (JPA entities, some binders), not domain value objects.
Enum vs constants class vs sealed interface: how do you model a fixed set?

| static final constants | enum | sealed interface + records
Type safety | None: any int or String fits | Yes | Yes
Instances | Values | Fixed singletons | Any number, each with its own data
Per-case data | No | Same fields for every constant | Different fields per subtype
Exhaustive switch | No | Yes | Yes (Java 21 pattern matching)
Example | Config limits | BloodType, Status | Payment = Card(no) | Upi(vpa) | Cash()
Rule of thumb: if every case is one fixed value, use an enum. If each case carries different data, use a sealed interface with record implementations. Use plain constants only for numbers or strings that are not a closed set of choices.
final reference vs unmodifiable view vs immutable object: what does each guarantee?

| final List<X> l | Collections.unmodifiableList(l) | List.copyOf(l) / immutable class
Can the variable be reassigned | No | Depends on the variable | Depends on the variable
Can you add or remove through it | Yes | No (UnsupportedOperationException) | No
Can the contents change underneath | Yes | Yes, through the original list | No
Are the elements themselves frozen | No | No | Only if the element type is immutable
Interview tip: final freezes a reference, not an object. An immutable class needs final fields, no setters, defensive copies in and out, and immutable components all the way down.
